overview: Kynance Cove is a small cove on the west side of the Lizard peninsula, about three kilometres north of Lizard Point. At low tide a sandy beach opens up between dark islands and stacks of serpentine rock, a stone that’s rare in Britain and gives the cove its colours.

It has drawn visitors since Victorian times, when Queen Victoria and Prince Albert came, and the National Trust now owns and looks after the cove and the surrounding cliffs, which are protected for their plants and geology.

expect.title: Tides matter
expect.text: Much of the sand and the paths between the rocks disappear at high tide, so check tide times and aim to be there around low water.

expect.title: The rocks
expect.text: Two kinds of serpentine meet here: the coarse, speckled rock you walk over on the way down, and the finer, banded stone of the islands and stacks in the cove.

expect.title: Café
expect.text: A café down at the cove has been serving visitors since 1929.

goodToKnow.label: Getting there
goodToKnow.text: There’s no road to the beach: park in the National Trust car park on the clifftop and follow the footpath down. The South West Coast Path runs along the cliffs above.

goodToKnow.label: Busy times
goodToKnow.text: It’s a small beach and fills up quickly on summer days.
